facts.title: Symbol from Latin
facts.text: Tin's chemical symbol Sn comes from its Latin name 'stannum'. The Latin word originally described an alloy of silver and lead before it came to mean tin specifically, while the English word 'tin' has separate ancient Germanic roots.

facts.title: It launched the Bronze Age
facts.text: Adding about 10% tin to copper produces bronze, an alloy far harder and more durable than either metal alone. This discovery, around 3300 BCE, transformed tools and weapons, and because tin ore is geographically rare it helped drive some of humanity's earliest long-distance trade networks.

facts.title: The eerie 'tin cry'
facts.text: Bend a bar of pure tin and you can hear a faint crackling sound known as the 'tin cry'. It is produced by the sudden rearrangement (twinning) of tin's crystal structure as the metal deforms.

facts.title: Tin pest turns it to dust
facts.text: Below about 13.2 °C ordinary silvery 'white tin' slowly converts into a crumbly grey powder called 'tin pest'. The change speeds up in deep cold and can make tin objects disintegrate, and it has long been blamed for crumbling buttons, coins and organ pipes in freezing climates.

facts.title: Tin cans barely contain tin
facts.text: A 'tin can' is actually made of steel coated with an extremely thin protective layer of tin that resists corrosion and keeps food safe. The actual tin makes up only a tiny fraction of the can's weight.

facts.title: It makes flat window glass
facts.text: Most flat glass is produced by the float-glass process, in which molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin. Because the glass floats and spreads evenly on the perfectly smooth liquid metal, it cools into flawlessly flat sheets.

facts.title: Champion of stable isotopes
facts.text: Tin has ten stable isotopes — more than any other element on the periodic table. This unusual stability comes from having 50 protons, a nuclear 'magic number' that makes the nucleus especially tightly bound.

facts.title: A superconductor for giant magnets
facts.text: The compound niobium-tin (Nb3Sn) becomes superconducting when cooled and is used to wind extremely powerful electromagnets. These magnets appear in MRI scanners and in fusion experiments such as the ITER reactor.

facts.title: The metal that holds electronics together
facts.text: Tin is the main ingredient in solder, the fusible metal that bonds components onto circuit boards. Old solder was a tin-lead mix, but modern electronics largely use lead-free tin-silver-copper alloys for safety.

facts.title: Two faces: alpha and beta
facts.text: Tin is allotropic, meaning it exists in different solid forms: brittle grey 'alpha' tin with a diamond-like structure, and the familiar malleable silvery 'beta' tin that is stable at room temperature. The transition between them is exactly what causes tin pest.
